issues.issue: The preamble dates the Agreement "as of" December 29, 2006, which cannot be squared with Paragraph 1's term "commencing on March 23, 2006" — nine months before the instrument was made. A court would have to decide whether the agreement operates retroactively to March 2006 or only from execution.

The stated duration is internally inconsistent: "approximately one (1) year and eight (8) months" does not match a term running from March 23, 2006 to midnight December 31, 2007, which is over twenty-one months. The mismatch, together with a start date preceding the December 29, 2006 execution date, leaves the actual commencement and length of the term open to construction.

The duty to "perform such other duties that are customarily performed by Managing Agents" and to manage "in a manner equal to the standard of competent office building managers in the Indianapolis greater metropolitan area" supplies no measurable boundary for either the scope of duties or the standard of care. A court would have to construe what customary duties and what competence standard the parties adopted.

"Due diligence" in collecting rents and other receivables is undefined and the Agreement sets no benchmark — no obligation to sue, to serve notices, or to report delinquencies — against which the effort could be measured. The phrase is vague as to what collection activity satisfies it.

"Contract for favorable terms, quality and service considered, ... as required" is vague as to whose judgment of "favorable" and "required" governs, and "out of the funds available" leaves unclear what happens when funds are short of the charges to be discharged. Both phrases would have to be construed to fix the Managing Agent's purchasing obligation.

The $1,000 expenditure cap is undone by two open-ended carve-outs in the same subparagraph: an emergency exception defined solely by what "the Managing Agent shall deem to be an emergency," and a sentence saying written approval is not required "for all reasonable expenditures" in listed categories, whose "all/reasonable" wording is ambiguous in scope. A court would have to decide whether the cap constrains anything beyond discretionary alterations.

This subparagraph is lettered "(d)" although the preceding subparagraph is also "(d)," so every later letter in Paragraph 2 is displaced by one and the cross-references elsewhere (Paragraph 3(a)'s references to "Paragraph 2(a)" and "Paragraph 2(c)") no longer land on the intended text. The mislettering makes it uncertain which subparagraph any cross-reference designates.

The promise that Principal "agrees to pay such excess promptly upon demand" whenever disbursements exceed receipts cannot easily be squared with Paragraph 2(d), which forbids expenditures over $1,000 without authorization, or with Paragraph 3(a), which bars reimbursement of the Agent's overhead. A court would have to decide whether Principal must fund a shortfall generated by unauthorized or non-reimbursable spending.

The subparagraph directs the reader to "Paragraph 3(a)" for the personnel-expense arrangement, but Paragraph 3(a) in turn describes personnel expenses "as provided in Paragraph 2(a)" — a subparagraph that says nothing about personnel — so the two cross-references point past each other. Which text actually governs reimbursement for personnel furnished by an Agent-controlled entity is left to construction.

Charging "office supplies, floor plans, any printed forms, advertising and other expenses identified with the Buildings" to Building operating expense sits against Paragraph 3(a), which makes the Agent's overhead — expressly including its bookkeeping, computer and phone systems — non-reimbursable, and against the first sentence here requiring the Agent to maintain its office at its own expense. A court would have to draw the line between Agent overhead and Building operating expense.

The annual estimate is "subject to the approval of Principal," but the provision states no standard for approval, no deadline, and no consequence if approval is withheld. Whether an unapproved budget suspends the Agent's spending authority under Paragraph 2(d) is left unstated.

The indemnity covers acts "taken or admitted to be taken," an apparent typographical error for "omitted," which changes the class of conduct indemnified. A court would have to decide whether omissions are within the indemnity at all.

The overhead exclusion says the Agent's non-reimbursable overhead "shall include any premiums on any insurance carried for its protection ... but shall include any premium on any insurance carried to protect any liability of another legal entity employing the personnel" — the second "shall include" is plainly meant to be "shall not include," and as written the sentence contradicts itself. Whether premiums for the affiliated employing entity are reimbursable turns entirely on repairing that word.

Its two cross-references misfire: personnel expenses are said to be "as provided in Paragraph 2(a)," which concerns management standards rather than personnel, and the monthly accounting is said to be "under the terms of Paragraph 2(c)," which concerns supplies and liens, the accounting duty actually sitting in the mislettered subparagraph 2(e). A court would have to identify the intended provisions before applying the reimbursement and set-off rules.
